title: Yoga, the boat to Brahman
hook: seekers ask where everything comes from, and the Shvetashvatara answers by teaching them to sit: the body as a boat to Brahman
carry: yoga is the boat to brahman

segments.voice: Yesterday: arani, the fire sticks. God is in you like fire in wood, and steady churning brings it out.
screen: `GOD IS IN YOU LIKE FIRE IN WOOD.`

segments.voice: A circle of seekers once sat together with the biggest questions there are. What is the cause of everything? Where do we come from? What holds our lives up? The Shvetashvatara Upanishad opens with them. And here's the turn: they didn't settle it by arguing. Following the yoga of meditation, the text says, they saw God's own power hidden in the world. So when this book teaches you how to sit, it isn't a fitness tip. It's the seekers' boat.
screen: `WHERE DO WE COME FROM?` → `THEY SAT.` → `THEY SAW.` → `THE BODY IS A BOAT.`

segments.voice: Chapter two gives the instructions. Verse 2.8, in paraphrase: holding the body steady, chest, neck and head upright, and drawing the senses and the mind into the heart, the wise one crosses the frightening rivers on the boat of Brahman. Verse 2.9 takes the breath: quiet it, and breathe out through the nose once it has grown soft. Then hold the mind the way a driver holds a chariot yoked to wild horses, alert, never careless. Verse 2.10 chooses the place: level and clean, free of pebbles, fire and sand, pleasing to the mind, near the sound of water, sheltered from the wind. Charmingly human: no gravel under you, no smoke in your eyes. Here's the teaching. The word yoga comes from a root meaning to yoke, to join, the same yoking as those horses. In Hinduism the straight spine and the soft breath were never the goal. They settle the body so the senses can turn inward, toward the self and toward God. The posture is the boat; Brahman is the far shore. The book closes by naming its teacher, the sage Shvetashvatara, who, it says, knew Brahman through his discipline and the grace of God, and passed it on. So a yoga class at the gym can be just exercise, and that's fine. But in this tradition, sitting still was always meant to carry you across.
screen: `CHEST, NECK, HEAD: UPRIGHT.` · `BREATH SOFT, GROUND LEVEL AND CLEAN.` · `YOKED, THE SENSES TURN INWARD.` · then, large: `THE BOAT OF BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Stack the three, chest lifted, neck long, head balanced on top, and let the breath grow soft and leave through the nose. Then gather the senses in, as if eyes, ears and skin were drawing back toward the heart. If a horse bolts, a thought or a sound, take the reins gently. If you pray, let the stillness carry you toward the one you pray to; if you don't, let the breath be the boat.
Asana, seat, posture. In the Shvetashvatara, the steady seat that becomes a boat: upright from chest to head, senses drawn into the heart.
Your line: yoga is the boat to Brahman. The body steady, the mind turned in. That's day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Hindus who meditate may sit cross-legged or on a chair with the chest, neck and head in one line, choose a clean, quiet corner, and soften the breath before turning attention inward, much as Shvetashvatara 2.8–2.10 describes.

fork.setup: a friend's yoga teacher says yoga is 'just stretching, nothing spiritual'. what would the Shvetashvatara add?
options: the posture is a boat: body steady, senses gathered, mind turned toward Brahman.
that yoga is only for priests, so nobody else should do it.
that the deeper the stretch, the closer you get to God.
fork.reveal: 2.8: with the body upright and the senses drawn into the heart, the wise cross the frightening rivers on the boat of Brahman. the seat serves the crossing.

original.note: Sanskrit āsana: seat, posture. the word the Yoga Sutras will later define as 'steady and comfortable'.

trapdoor: what you thought: posture is a modern add-on to old spiritual ideas.
what it means: this Upanishad's meditation teaching begins with the spine, the breath and the room.
what a scholar hears: 2.9's mind held like a chariot yoked to unruly horses echoes the Katha's chariot (1.3.3–1.3.6), and 2.13 even lists the first signs of progress.

tie.story: In the Shvetashvatara, seekers asking where everything comes from turn to meditation, and the teacher shows them how: sit upright, gather the senses into the heart, and cross the frightening rivers on the boat of Brahman.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam his class can be just exercise, and that for Hindus the stillness was always meant to carry you somewhere.
tie.you: where does your mind go when your body finally sits still?

Katha.meaning: an Upanishad that pictures the senses as horses

Brahman.meaning: the great reality; here, a boat across the rivers

Shvetashvatara.meaning: the Upanishad of the wheel, the swan and the fire sticks

yoga.meaning: from a root meaning to yoke or join; a discipline that turns the mind inward

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.1–1.3 (the seekers' questions; through the yoga of meditation they saw God's own power)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 2.8 (body upright, senses into the heart, the boat of Brahman)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 2.9 (the breath; the mind like a chariot with wild horses)
Katha Upanishad 1.3.3–1.3.6 (the chariot and the horses)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.21 (Shvetashvatara knew Brahman by the power of his austerity and the grace of God, and taught it)

notes: Date: 'more than two thousand years old by most estimates' (the Shvetashvatara is usually placed in the last centuries BCE). Confirm phrasing.
'One of the earliest descriptions of sitting meditation in Hindu scripture': widely stated; the Katha also has early yoga material. Please check.
2.10 list (pebbles, fire, sand/gravel; sound of water; not offensive to the eye; sheltered from wind) follows Müller/Hume; confirm.
